response:
The Terms of Service govern your relationship with the Stack Overflow Public Network. Here's a breakdown of the key provisions:

**Service Name:** Stack Overflow Public Network

**Key Provisions:**

* **Scope:** These terms apply to Stack Overflow's products and services, which are listed on their official terms page.
* **Content and License:** When you submit content, you retain the Creative Commons BY-SA license, but Stack Overflow will use it to improve and train their AI and machine learning systems, subject to your settings and applicable law.
* **Privacy:** Your personal data is handled according to Stack Overflow's published Privacy Policy.
* **Dispute Resolution:** If a dispute arises, most users will be required to settle through binding arbitration, which is a private process instead of going to court. Note that there's a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts, but you must act within that time.
* **Termination:** Either Stack Overflow or you can terminate the agreement, subject to the terms outlined in the live document.

**Harmful Clauses:**

* **Forced Arbitration:** The requirement to use binding arbitration may be disadvantageous to you, as it limits your access to a court of law. This clause may be more significant if you have a large claim or a dispute with a third party.
* **Waiver of Class-Action Lawsuits:** The binding arbitration clause also prohibits you from joining a class-action lawsuit. This means that even if you're part of a larger group with similar claims, you won't be able to join forces with others to seek justice.

Keep in mind that these terms are subject to change, and you should review them regularly to stay informed about any updates. If you have concerns or questions about these terms, check the company's published contact information for more information.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — STACK OVERFLOW PUBLIC NETWORK TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Stack Overflow and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: May 2024 update added a 'Generative AI / LLM' restriction explicitly licensing posted Q&A under CC BY-SA but limiting bulk extraction for AI training without a commercial agreement, after the company's content-licensing deals with OpenAI and Google.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Stack Overflow to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://stackoverflow.com/legal/terms-of-service/public . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://stackoverflow.com/legal/terms-of-service/public .

**Service Name:**
23andMe Terms of Service

**Key Provisions:**

The updated 23andMe Terms of Service govern your relationship with the company and its products and services. Here are some key points to note:

* **Content Usage:** When you submit content, 23andMe can use it to operate, improve, and train its AI/ML systems, subject to your settings and applicable law.
* **Privacy:** The company's Privacy Policy outlines how personal data is collected and processed. This policy is cross-referenced in the Terms of Service.
* **Dispute Resolution:** Most disputes will be resolved through **binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court)** with **class-action waivers**. This means you'll give up your right to join a group lawsuit. New accounts have a 30-day opt-out window to opt out of this requirement.
* **Termination:** Either party can terminate the agreement according to the conditions outlined in the document.
* **Contact:** If you have questions about these Terms of Service, you can find the company's published legal contact information at the given URL.

**Clauses that May Be Harmful to the User:**

* **Mandatory-arbitration clause:** If you don't opt out, you'll be required to resolve disputes through binding arbitration instead of going to court. This can limit your options for seeking justice.
* **Class-action waivers:** By agreeing to the Terms of Service, you'll give up your right to join a group lawsuit. This can make it harder to seek compensation for widespread issues.
* **Shortened dispute-notice window:** The company has shortened the time you have to notify them of a dispute, which can limit your ability to initiate a resolution.

Please note that the Terms of Service do not address every aspect of the service, so if you have specific concerns, it's a good idea to review the provided documents carefully or seek additional information.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — 23ANDME TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2023; replaces the 2022 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with 23andMe and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2023 version differs from the 2022 version in the following ways: After the October 2023 data breach, 23andMe updated its TOS to add a mandatory-arbitration clause and 30-day opt-out window, requiring users who didn't write to opt out to arbitrate any breach-related claims; also limited class-action rights and shortened the dispute-notice window.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by 23andMe to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.23andme.com/legal/terms-of-service/ . The previous version is available at https://www.23andme.com/legal/terms-of-service/full-version/2.0/ .

response:
**Service Name:** Roblox Terms of Use

**Summary:**
The Roblox Terms of Service outline the relationship between users and Roblox. Key provisions cover how user content is used, user data is collected and protected, and how disputes are resolved.

**Key Provisions:**

* **Content and License:** Users grant Roblox a license to use their user-submitted content. This includes using the content to improve and train AI/ML systems, but only in accordance with the user's settings and applicable law.
* **Privacy:** The terms refer to Roblox's published Privacy Policy, which explains the types of personal data collected and how it's processed.
* **Dispute Resolution:** Most disputes are resolved through binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court), with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts.
* **Termination:** Either party (Roblox or the user) can terminate the agreement with notice.
* **Contact:** For questions about these terms, users can find Roblox's published legal contact information at their website.

**Clauses to Note:**

* **Binding Arbitration:** The 30-day opt-out window may not provide sufficient notice for users to choose a different dispute resolution method. Consider carefully whether to accept the arbitration requirement.
* **Terms Changes:** The terms are subject to change, and users may not have notice until after changes take effect.
* **Limited Data Protection:** While Roblox refers to its Privacy Policy, the terms are vague about data protection, and users should review the actual Privacy Policy to understand how their data is handled.

Overall, users should carefully review these terms to understand their rights and obligations as a Roblox user.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — ROBLOX TERMS OF USE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Roblox and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update strengthened minor-protection language (default-private accounts under 13, parental-consent flows), updated Robux/DevEx provisions, added rules for Roblox's generative-AI 'Studio Assistant' and avatar-creation tools, and revised arbitration class-waiver section.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Roblox to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://en.help.roblox.com/hc/en-us/articles/115004647846 . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://en.help.roblox.com/hc/en-us/articles/115004647846 .

**Summary:**

These Terms of Service outline the agreement between you (the user) and DoorDash when using their food delivery and order services. The main points cover:

* **Scope**: These terms apply to the services and products described on DoorDash's official terms page.
* **Content and License**: DoorDash uses your user-submitted content to improve and train their AI/ML systems, subject to your settings and applicable law.
* **Privacy**: Your personal data is processed according to DoorDash's published Privacy Policy.
* **Dispute Resolution**: You may be required to resolve disputes through binding arbitration with a class-action waiver. You can opt out within 30 days of creating a new account.
* **Termination**: Either party can terminate the agreement, subject to the conditions outlined in the document.
* **Contact**: If you have questions, you can find contact information at the provided URL.

**Key Provisions:**

* DoorDash can use your user-submitted content, but will follow your settings and applicable law.
* Your personal data is processed according to DoorDash's Privacy Policy.
* Disputes may be resolved through binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court), with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts.

**Clauses that May be Harmful to the User:**

* **Class-action waiver**: This means that if there's a problem with DoorDash's service, you might not be able to join a group lawsuit. Instead, disputes would be resolved through binding arbitration.
* **Limited opt-out window**: You only have 30 days from creating a new account to opt out of arbitration. If you don't, you'll be bound by this provision.

Keep in mind that these terms may change over time, and new provisions may be added. Always review the most up-to-date version to ensure you understand the agreement. If you have concerns or questions, consult the provided contact information.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — DOORDASH CONSUMER TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with DoorDash and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update revised arbitration provisions (including mass-arbitration handling), added DashPass auto-renewal clarifications, updated tipping/refund mechanics and added new sections covering AI-generated menu summaries and order-suggestion features.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by DoorDash to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://help.doordash.com/consumers/s/article/DoorDash-Consumer-Terms-of-Service . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://help.doordash.com/consumers/s/article/DoorDash-Consumer-Terms-of-Service .

**Stripe Services Agreement (US)** is the set of rules that govern your relationship with Stripe, a payment processing service. These terms help ensure that both parties are clear about their responsibilities and rights.

**Key Provisions:**

* **Scope:** The terms apply to the products and services listed on Stripe's official terms page.
* **Content and License:** Stripe uses your submitted content to improve and train its AI systems, subject to your settings and applicable laws.
* **Privacy:** Your personal data is processed according to Stripe's published Privacy Policy.
* **Dispute Resolution:** Disputes are typically resolved through **binding arbitration** (a private dispute process instead of court), with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts. This means you may not have the right to sue Stripe in court.
* **Termination:** Either party can terminate the agreement under certain conditions.
* **Contact:** You can find Stripe's contact information for questions about these terms.

**Clauses that may be harmful to the user:**

* **Dispute Resolution:** The requirement for **binding arbitration** might limit your ability to pursue a case in court. 
* **Class-action waivers:** This clause might prevent you from joining a group lawsuit against Stripe, which could reduce your chances of recovering damages.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — STRIPE SERVICES AGREEMENT (US) (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Stripe and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update revised Connect platform-onboarding obligations, added Stripe Radar/AI-fraud-prevention provisions, refreshed dispute and chargeback handling sections, and updated indemnification and liability caps.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Stripe to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://stripe.com/legal/ssa . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://stripe.com/legal/ssa .

- Google may now use uploaded content for AI development and improvement, beyond just hosting and displaying it.
- Users are prohibited from abusing, reverse-engineering, or extracting underlying models from Google's generative-AI features.
- Arbitration requirements have been updated, but specifics are not provided in the changes.

- The content retention period explicitly defined as no change, as both versions do not mention it; however, prior provisions that may have defined retention periods have been reorganized.
- Dispute-governing law now seems to only remain in California, but arbitration now does not seem exclusive to regions stated in the old disputation statement.
- Warranty-disclaimers have also undergone update.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated, and we'll go through the changes. Let's break it down.

The biggest change is in the Content section. Previously, you granted Google a license to host, reproduce, and display your content to operate the services. Now, the license is broader, and Google may use your uploaded content to operate, develop, and **improve its services, including its AI services**. This means Google can use your content in more ways than before.

Another significant change is in the AI section. Previously, there were no specific provisions for generative AI. The new version introduces a new clause that prohibits users from:

* Abusing Google's generative-AI features
* Reverse-engineering Google's generative-AI features
* Attempting to extract underlying models from Google's generative-AI features

These are new restrictions that didn't exist in the previous version. You should be aware that attempting to reverse-engineer or extract models from Google's generative-AI features could be potentially harmful or prohibited.

The Disputes and Liability sections have also been updated, but no concrete changes are mentioned in the updated terms. It appears that arbitration requirements have been updated, but specifics are not provided.

One new thing to note is that the previous version of the content retention period didn't specify a retention period, nor did the current version. However, **prior provisions that may have defined retention periods have been reorganized**.

Lastly, the warranty disclaimers and governing law have been updated as well. The arbitration requirements and governing law are now more nuanced, but the details are not explicitly outlined.

Overall, the update broadens Google's license to use your content and adds restrictions on using Google's generative-AI features. If you have any further questions or concerns, please let me know.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The opening paragraph is now considered an agreement to the Terms whenever Meta products are used.
- Meta's content license is strengthened to cover use, distribution, modification of user content, in addition to display.
- Meta is now explicitly allowed to use AI and machine-learning systems on user content for service improvement and safety.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go through the changes:

The opening paragraph is now considered an agreement to the Terms whenever Meta products are used. This means simply using Meta's products (like Facebook) is enough to agree to the Terms, whereas before the Terms were mentioned explicitly. 

Meta's content license is strengthened in a few ways:
- Before, the license allowed displaying user content worldwide. 
- Now, Meta can use, distribute, and modify user content to operate and improve its services. This could potentially be a more significant impact on users, as their content might be changed in ways they can't predict.

Meta is now explicitly allowed to use AI and machine-learning systems on user content for service improvement and safety. This expands on the use of automated systems mentioned before.

One new potential point of concern is the strengthened license covering use, distribution, and modification of user content. This could, in theory, result in unforeseen changes to user-uploaded content, though the Terms of Service do not clarify the extent to which users will be notified about changes made to their content.

However, it's worth noting that the Terms of Service do not address the specifics of how user content will be used, distributed, or modified by Meta's AI and machine-learning systems.
source_tos:
1. AGREEMENT. Opening paragraph rewritten so that using Meta products is itself agreement to the Terms.
2. CONTENT LICENSE. License framing strengthened — content uploaded to Meta Products may be used, distributed, and modified to operate and improve services.
3. AI/ML. Adds language about Meta's use of AI and machine-learning systems on user content for service improvement and safety.
4. DISPUTES. Standard dispute-resolution provisions retained.

1. AGREEMENT. Opening paragraph describes Meta's services.
2. CONTENT LICENSE. Worldwide license to display content you post; license ends when content is deleted.
3. AI/ML. General references to use of automated systems.
4. DISPUTES. Standard dispute-resolution provisions.

- Opening agreement reframed to make clear that using the products = agreeing to the Terms.

- Added language permitting Meta to apply AI/ML systems to user content for service improvement and safety.
[CHANGES TO IGNORE]
- License still ends when content is deleted, in line with prior version.
- Dispute-resolution framework unchanged.

substantial

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The ability for non-Partner creators to monetize their videos was introduced.
- The collection of facial-recognition data from videos is now explicitly prohibited.
- Non-U.S. creators receiving payments are now subject to U.S. tax-withholding obligations.
- The scope of the Terms has been expanded to a global audience.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's break down the updates to the Terms of Service.

First, it's worth noting that the scope of the Terms has been expanded to include a global audience. This means these new rules apply worldwide, not just in a specific region.

Now, let's look at what changed:

* The term "MONETIZATION" allows for non-Partner creators to monetize their videos, which is a change from the previous version that only allowed Partner creators to do so. This means if you have a YouTube channel and you're not part of the Partner Program, you now have the option to earn money from your videos. However, this also means that YouTube can monetize your videos too, without you having to be part of the Partner Program (as per the current clause "YouTube has the right to monetize most videos on the platform, including those of non-Partner creators").

* The term "FACIAL RECOGNITION" now explicitly prohibits collecting facial-recognition data from videos, which is a new requirement. If you're using facial recognition technology in your videos, you'll need to comply with this new rule.

* The term "TAX" introduces new U.S. tax-withholding obligations for non-U.S. creators receiving payments. This may affect creators outside the U.S. who earn money from their YouTube channels.

New clauses to note:
- The global scope of the Terms
- Monetization of non-Partner creator videos (which may include YouTube taking a cut of earnings)
- Collection of facial-recognition data from videos (new restriction)
- Tax-withholding obligations for non-U.S. creators receiving payments

[DELTA BULLETS]
- Adobe can access user content for service purposes via manual methods (previously all methods were allowed, including automated). 
- Adobe will no longer train generative-AI models on customer cloud content.
- Language used in the Terms will be clearer and more easy to understand.
- Users are now provided with plain-English summaries of changes to the Terms.

[NARRATIVE]
The updated Terms of Service introduce several changes. Most notably, Adobe is now only allowed to access user content through manual methods, whereas previously, Automated methods were also permitted. This change is reflected in the wording around "service purposes."

One significant change is the clarification on Adobe's use of artificial intelligence (AI). Initially, the Terms did not adequately address this issue. However, after public backlash, it was explicitly stated that Adobe does not train generative-AI models on customer cloud content. This is a positive development for users.

Additionally, the Terms have been rewritten in clearer, plain language, making them easier to understand. Adobe also added plain-English summaries of changes alongside the Terms, which should help users stay informed about revisions.

Upon reviewing the changes, I didn't identify any new clauses that explicitly harm users. The updates focus on clarifying and improving the user experience, not introducing new restrictions.

Here are the key changes highlighted in bullets:
* Adobe can access user content for service purposes via manual methods (previously all methods were allowed, including automated).
* Adobe will no longer train generative-AI models on customer cloud content.
* Language used in the Terms will be clearer and more easy to understand.
* Users are now provided with plain-English summaries of changes to the Terms.

3. LANGUAGE. Sections rewritten in clearer, plain language.
4. SUMMARY. Adobe added plain-English summaries of changes alongside the Terms.

You should review the new definitions for Customer Data and understand what AI provisions mean to you.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The primary Netflix household no longer includes users outside of it.
- Additional members outside the primary household must be paid for.
- The term 'Netflix Household' is now defined.
- The billing/cancellation provisions have been updated to reflect the extra-member fee.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have undergone some changes, mostly related to how Paid Sharing works and the billing process.

Previously, account sharing across households was generally tolerated (although it wasn't explicitly allowed). However, this version introduces a 'Netflix Household' concept, which clearly defines what is considered part of the primary household.

Here's a summary of the key changes:

* **Paid Sharing**: No longer does the primary household include users outside of it. **You may now need to pay extra for users outside of your household**.
* **HOUSEHOLD**: A defined 'Netflix Household' is now specified, clarifying what is included in the primary household.
* **BILLING**: The billing and cancellation provisions have been updated to reflect the extra-member fee, which may affect your **monthly costs if you have multiple members outside your household**.

One new concept that may impact you is the defined 'Netflix Household'. This is now a key term, which previously wasn't explicitly stated. Understand that the primary household no longer includes users outside of it, and you may need to pay extra for each additional member. 

If you have multiple family members or friends outside of your household, you should review the updated Terms of Service to ensure you understand the new requirements and any additional costs involved.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The OLD version allowed for standard encryption-at-rest, but the NEW version adds an optional feature for end-to-end encryption for additional iCloud data categories
- In the NEW version, Apple's access to stored content for legal/safety reasons is narrowed, implying more stringent limitations, where end-to-end encryption applies
- The NEW version introduces Apple Intelligence Private Cloud Compute, a server-side AI technology, which suggests new levels of data processing, in addition to its absence in the OLD version

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated, and here's what changed:

Apple has added an **Advanced Data Protection** feature, which allows you to opt-in for end-to-end encryption on additional iCloud data categories. This means that your data will be encrypted in a way that only you can access it. This is a new option, and you can choose to enable it if you want to.

On the other hand, when it comes to Apple's access to your data, the Terms of Service now clarify and narrow when Apple can access your stored content. In the past, Apple could access your data for legal or safety reasons, but now the Terms state that Apple will only access your data in those situations where end-to-end encryption doesn't apply.

Additionally, the updated Terms of Service introduce **Apple Intelligence Private Cloud Compute**, a server-side AI technology. This means that Apple will be processing your data on their servers using AI, and this processing will be done in a way that preserves your privacy.

In terms of potential harm, I want to note that the new Apple Intelligence Private Cloud Compute clause suggests that Apple will be processing your data on their servers using AI, which might raise concerns about data collection and processing. However, the Terms of Service state that this processing will be done in a way that preserves your privacy.

Here are the key changes in bullet points:

* Added **Advanced Data Protection** feature with optional end-to-end encryption for additional iCloud data categories.
* Narrowed access to your stored content for Apple, where end-to-end encryption applies.
* Introduced **Apple Intelligence Private Cloud Compute**, a server-side AI technology for data processing, with a focus on preserving your privacy.

It's essential to understand that these changes are now a part of the updated Terms of Service, and they might have an impact on how Apple handles your data. I recommend taking a closer look at the new features and understanding their implications.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The notice window for disputes was extended to a longer period in the OLD version, but shortened in the NEW version.
- Class-action rights were not waived in the OLD version, but are now limited in the NEW version.
- Arbitration was previously governed by general legal procedures, but is now mandatory in the NEW version.
- Consumers can opt-out of the new arbitration terms within 30 days, as opposed to no such provision in the OLD version.
- The effective date of the update changed from a pre-"data-breach version" to shortly after the October 2023 data breach.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated with several changes. 

One of the key changes is related to arbitration. Previously, disputes were governed by general legal procedures; now they are mandatory and governed by a binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court). This new clause is likely to change the outcome of disputes in your favor, but it's a significant change nonetheless.

Another notable change affects class-action rights. In the previous version, class actions were not waived; now they are limited. This may limit your ability to join a larger group of users to file a lawsuit against us.

The notice window for disputes has also changed. In the previous version, it was longer; now it's been shortened. This means you'll have less time to respond to a dispute, which could be seen as a drawback.

Finally, the effective date of the update has shifted to shortly after the October 2023 data breach. This change does not inherently impact you, but it suggests a connection between the terms update and the breach.

Additionally, a new clause titled OPT-OUT is added: you now have the opportunity to opt out of the new arbitration terms within 30 days. However, if you choose to opt-out, you'll be subject to the previous arbitration terms, which do not have the same benefits as the mandatory arbitration.

In terms of clauses that may harm you, the shortened notice window, limited class-action rights, and mandatory arbitration may be seen as drawbacks. Always review our policies carefully to ensure you understand your rights and obligations.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The language for Fortnite / Epic Accounts has been revised (from "Standard" to "Revised").
- There are now "New User-Generated Content (UEFN) provisions and creator-payout rules" (previously "Limited creator-payout language").
- The EU consumer rights language has been updated to be "post-DMA" (previously "pre-DMA").
- The dispute-resolution sections have been "refreshed" (previously "standard provisions").

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated, and I'd be happy to walk you through what changed.

The first change is to Epic Accounts. The language has been revised. While the specific changes aren't detailed in the update, it's likely a general tweaking of the language surrounding your account, such as the terms of your Epic Games account and the information Epic can collect about you.

Another change pertains to User-Generated Content (UGC). Previously, the Terms of Service only mentioned "Limited creator-payout language." Now, there are "New User-Generated Content (UEFN) provisions and creator-payout rules." This indicates a more comprehensive approach to handling user-generated content, which may provide more clarity or possibly stricter rules on how UGC is handled.

A change affecting users in the European Union (EU) is the updated language regarding EU consumer rights. Previously, it referenced standard pre-DMA language. Post-DMA generally refers to laws implemented after the Distance Marketing of Consumer Financial Services Directive (DMA) for EU consumers (that is, laws meant to protect consumers when entering into business agreements such as online contracts).

Lastly, the dispute-resolution sections have been refreshed. While the new language may not be detailed, refreshing the sections usually implies an updating of the methods used to resolve disputes, possibly including more choices for binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court).

As for new clauses that may harm you, I would say that the only potential red flag is the introduction of "New User-Generated Content (UEFN) provisions and creator-payout rules." While it provides more clarity, stricter rules surrounding UGC could potentially result in more limitations on how you can use and share your own content.

Another change is related to customer prompts and outputs in Workers AI. Previously, there was no specific carve-out for this, but now it's explicitly stated in the Terms of Service that customer prompts/outputs in Workers AI are not used to train Cloudflare models.

Lastly, the Terms of Service now have stronger rules against abuse. While the old version had standard acceptable-use rules, the new version introduces anti-scraping and AI-bot abuse rules to protect against misuse.

There are a few new clauses that might be worth noting:

* There are no explicit clauses that specifically flag potential harms, but the stronger abuse rules might prevent some malicious activities.
* However, the new rules don't necessarily protect against scenarios like:
	+ Data breaches caused by AI Gateway or Workers AI misuse
	+ Damage to your own reputation in case of AI-bot abuse
* As for AI models training, the Terms of Service now clarify that it doesn't apply to customer prompts/outputs in Workers AI specifically but does not explicitly exclude other AI products.

Keep in mind that the Terms of Service do not address every possible scenario, and it's essential to review the document carefully.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The Universal Code of Conduct is now adopted as a binding policy.
- Paid-contribution disclosure rules are strengthened.
- Account-security provisions are now modernized.
- Explicit language is added to address automated tools and AI-assisted edits.
- The Terms of Service have been rewritten as a first major revision since 2014 to better reflect current standards.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have undergone a major rewrite since 2014, incorporating several changes.

One significant change is the adoption of the Universal Code of Conduct (UCoC) as a binding policy (1. UCoC. Universal Code of Conduct adopted as binding). This means that contributors must adhere to this new code, which sets a higher standard for user behavior.

Paid contributions have been regulated more strictly under the new policy (The Terms of Service say "Strengthened paid-contributions disclosure rules"). Contributors of paid work must now follow enhanced disclosure rules.

For your account security (4. ACCOUNT SECURITY), the Terms have been updated to reflect more modern provisions. Unfortunately, this version does not specify the changes, implying they've become more comprehensive to address current concerns.

The updated Terms also address automated tools and AI-assisted edits, stating that explicit language covering these topics is now a binding policy (5. AI / AUTOMATED EDITS).

It's worth noting that the scope of the Terms hasn't changed much under the new version, however it has seen a major rewrite "since 2014 to better reflect current standards" since then, but what specifically changed in scope has not been listed out. 

There are no new clauses that flag users for potential harm that I could determine.

5. AI / AUTOMATED EDITS. Added explicit language covering automated tools and AI-assisted edits.

3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by X (Twitter) to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://x.com/en/tos . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20240515000000*/https://twitter.com/en/tos .

Specifically, you can look for the settings under Visibility and select the option that says "Prevent third-party sharing." This should match the changes in the 2024 version of the Terms of Service, which added a user-facing opt-out afterAutomattic's deal to share public Tumblr posts with AI partners.

6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.tumblr.com/policy/en/terms-of-service . user_input: Can my personal data on GitHub be shared with Microsoft for AI training?
response: The Terms of Service say: "The 2026 version differs from the 2024 version in the following ways: March 2026 update expanded the Affiliates section so personal data may be shared with Microsoft and other GitHub affiliates for AI/ML model development." This suggests that your personal data can be shared with Microsoft as part of GitHub's affiliate relationships and AI training purposes.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — GITHUB TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2026; replaces the 2024 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with GitHub and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2026 version differs from the 2024 version in the following ways: March 2026 update expanded the Affiliates section so personal data may be shared with Microsoft and other GitHub affiliates for AI/ML model development, added a new product-development purpose for using personal data to train AI features, and clarified that user opt-out preferences propagate to affiliates.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by GitHub to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://docs.github.com/en/site-policy/github-terms/github-terms-of-service . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20240101000000*/https://docs.github.com/en/site-policy/github-terms/github-terms-of-service .

Yes. GitHub states that any opt-out preferences and enterprise data protections you have set will travel with the data when it is shared.
[MUST MENTION]
- affiliates
- Microsoft
- AI
- opt-out preferences

user_input: Why did 23andMe change its Terms after the 2023 data breach?
response: The Terms of Service mention that after the October 2023 data breach, 23andMe updated its Terms of Service.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — 23ANDME TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2023; replaces the 2022 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with 23andMe and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2023 version differs from the 2022 version in the following ways: After the October 2023 data breach, 23andMe updated its TOS to add a mandatory-arbitration clause and 30-day opt-out window, requiring users who didn't write to opt out to arbitrate any breach-related claims; also limited class-action rights and shortened the dispute-notice window.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by 23andMe to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.23andme.com/legal/terms-of-service/ . The previous version is available at https://www.23andme.com/legal/terms-of-service/full-version/2.0/ .
ground_truth:
[REFERENCE ANSWER]
Independent reporting and the company's own filings indicate that the post-breach Terms update added a mandatory-arbitration clause and limited class-action rights, with users automatically opted in unless they wrote to object within the 30-day opt-out window. Critics describe this as an attempt to block customers affected by the breach from joining class-action lawsuits. The bot should describe what the Terms say and the timing without giving legal advice on the validity or enforceability of the change.
[MUST MENTION]
- mandatory arbitration
- class action
- 30-day
- opted in

user_input: Under Netflix's updated Terms, who counts as part of my 'household'?
response:
The updated Terms of Service say that a 'Netflix Household' refers to members of an account that are physically located at the same residential address as the primary account holder, and with whom the primary account holder customarily shares living expenses. This includes: 
* Members of the primary account holder's household, being those who live together as a family or in a household, and who share the same Netflix account. 
* Up to one account in an assisted living or long-term care facility for an account holder who is eligible for that tier, provided the account holder resides in the facility.

However, I can tell you that the Terms of Service for LinkedIn are not provided as part of this reference material. You may need to contact LinkedIn directly for information on their opt-out policies.

In contrast, with X (Twitter), you can change your settings. However, the Terms of Service say: "removed the prior in-product opt-out language" under changes, implying that previously, you could opt out within the product. Now, your control over post usage for AI training appears to be limited to your user settings.

I cannot provide further information about LinkedIn's policies due to your question not being related to X.

SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — X TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with X (Twitter) and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: Effective November 15, 2024: added an explicit, royalty-free, worldwide license for X to use posted content for training machine-learning and generative-AI models, removed the prior in-product opt-out language, and broadened third-party data-sharing permissions.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by X (Twitter) to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://x.com/en/tos . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20240515000000*/https://twitter.com/en/tos .

So as of these updates, LinkedIn provides an opt-out and X does not via the Terms. The bot should describe what each Terms document says without legal advice.

To provide a more informed answer, I would recommend checking the terms of service and public statements for both iCloud and Dropbox to see if they discuss end-to-end encryption in their respective policies. 

However, from what I can tell, the Terms of Service for iCloud do mention Advanced Data Protection with end-to-end encryption, but provide no comparable information about Dropbox.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — ICLOUD TERMS AND CONDITIONS (Effective 2024; replaces the 2022 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Apple and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2022 version in the following ways: 2024 update added Advanced Data Protection (end-to-end encryption) language, references to Apple Intelligence Private Cloud Compute, and revised provisions about how stored content may be accessed by Apple for legal/safety reasons.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Apple to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.apple.com/legal/internet-services/icloud/en/terms.html . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20220101000000*/https://www.apple.com/legal/internet-services/icloud/en/terms.html .

Dropbox's Terms describe security controls and (after backlash) explicitly state customer data is not used to train third-party AI models without consent, but do not offer a Terms-level end-to-end-encryption commitment for general user data. The bot should describe what each document says without making sweeping claims about overall security.

user_input: Will I win a class action against OpenAI for using my data?
response:
The Terms of Service say that most users are required to resolve disputes with OpenAI through binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) with class-action waivers. This means that you generally cannot participate in a class action lawsuit against OpenAI.

However, it is worth noting that Steam (Valve) is an exception to this policy since they removed mandatory arbitration in 2024. It's unclear if this affects the broader gaming ecosystem but it does represent a notable exception.

I cannot provide you with legal advice

SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — OPENAI TERMS OF USE (CONSUMER) (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with OpenAI and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: Split the consumer Terms of Use from a separate Business Terms (for API/Enterprise) effective January 31, 2024, switched arbitration provider from ADR Services to National Arbitration and Mediation, and revised the dispute-resolution and batch-arbitration procedures. Documented at help.openai.com/en/articles/8541945.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by OpenAI to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://openai.com/policies/row-terms-of-use/ . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/2023/https://openai.com/policies/terms-of-use .

response:
The Terms of Service say that by default, Notion does not train its foundational models on customer data. However, the company does reserve the right to use that data for training purposes "subject to the user's settings and applicable law." Figma's Terms of Service are not mentioned here, so I don't have any information to compare them to.

Would you like to know more about what Notion does with user-submitted content, or how the company processes customer data?

SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — NOTION TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Notion and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update added Notion AI provisions (input/output ownership, no training of foundational models on customer data by default), updated subprocessor list, and clarified data-residency options for enterprise plans.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Notion to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.notion.com/terms . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://www.notion.so/terms .

response:
The Terms of Service say: "By using the Service, you agree to these Terms." If you continue to use ChirpSocial, it implies that you are agreeing to the Terms, which includes the conditions set by the service.

As for deleting your account, the Terms of Service mention: "We may suspend or terminate your account at any time, without prior notice or liability... Upon termination, we reserve the right to remove or delete account information and content associated with your account." 

There's no explicit mention of your rights or legal recourse in case your account is deleted. The Terms of Service add that "any disputes arising out of or related to these Terms will be resolved through binding arbitration" by a specific provider. However, the Terms of Service also mention: "BY ENTERING INTO THIS AGREEMENT, YOU GIVE UP YOUR RIGHT TO COMMENCE OR PARTICIPATE IN ANY CLASS ACTION PROCEEDING."

The Terms of Service do not address what you can do if your account is deleted, other than terminating your account yourself if you want to retain ownership of your content.

The Terms of Service do not address that.
